title: Salt bar soap
subtitle: A hard, polishing bar with 80% sea salt
excerpt: Salt bar soap is a cold-process bar with olive and coconut oils, with sea salt making up 80% of the oil weight stirred in at trace. The salt produces an exceptionally hard, dense bar that polishes and exfoliates gently in the shower and gives a tight, creamy lather. Makes seven bars; cut within six hours of pouring, the salt hardens the batter fast.
sourceNotes: Salt bar technique in Susan Miller Cavitch, The Natural Soap Book (1995) and The Soapmaker's Companion (1997). High coconut oil percentage (80%) is standard for salt bars to offset the hardening effect of the salt on lather. SAP values: coconut oil 0.190, olive oil 0.134. 20% superfat typical for salt bars to maintain conditioning. Salt at 80% of oil weight. Water as 33% of oil weight.

recipe.batchNotes: Salt bars must be cut within 6 hours of pouring; once the salt hardens the bar fully it cannot be cut cleanly. Do not attempt larger batches unless you can cut them in time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Salt bars cure faster than standard bars. Four weeks is sufficient; the salt keeps them naturally hard and long-lasting.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Three years or more in a cool dry cupboard. Salt preserves the bar and the high superfat resists rancidity. Discard if DOS (dreaded orange spots) or a paint-like smell appears.

glossaryTerms.definition: The percentage of fat left unreacted in the finished bar. Salt bars use a higher superfat than standard bars, typically 15 to 20%, because the salt hardens the bar so much that extra conditioning oil is needed to prevent the bar from feeling drying.
The point at which soap batter thickens so that a drizzle on the surface briefly holds its shape. Salt bars should be poured at a thin trace only, the salt accelerates hardening quickly once added.

projectSchedule.title: Cut within 6 hours
projectSchedule.body: Cut the bars within six hours of pouring, while the batter is firm but not yet rock-hard. If using a loaf mould, slice into bars. Individual silicone bar moulds remove the timing risk, the batter sets in the mould shape and no cutting is needed.

projectSchedule.title: Four-week cure complete
projectSchedule.body: Salt bars cure faster than standard bars. At four weeks the bar is very hard, pale, and ready to use. The lather is tight and dense rather than bubbly, this is characteristic.

content.text: Salt bar soap is a cold-process bar made with olive and coconut oils, with fine sea salt making up 80% of the oil weight stirred in at light
trace

. The salt makes the bar exceptionally hard and dense; it polishes and exfoliates gently in the shower and gives a tight, creamy lather. Makes seven bars; cut within six hours of pouring, the salt hardens the batter fast.
Wear protective gloves and goggles before handling lye. Weigh the salt before you start and have it ready to stir in immediately after trace; there is no time to weigh while the batter waits.
Ingredients

items.prepNote: 80% of oil weight; high coconut oil is standard for salt bars, it provides lather the salt would otherwise suppress
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 20% superfat on this oil blend, salt bars use a higher superfat than standard bars
80% of oil weight; fine-ground for an even texture in the bar; stirred in at trace

content.text: Method
Mix the lye solution
In a ventilated space, wearing gloves and goggles, pour the distilled water into the HDPE pitcher. Add the sodium hydroxide in a steady stream while stirring. Set aside to cool to 38 to 42°C.
Melt and prepare the oils
Melt the coconut oil over a low heat. Combine with the olive oil in a heatproof bowl. Cool to 38 to 42°C.
Blend to a thin trace, then add salt

Pour the lye solution into the oils. Stick-blend in short bursts until the batter is just at a thin trace, no thicker than thin cream. Stop blending immediately. Stir in the sea salt by hand quickly and thoroughly. The batter will thicken fast once the salt is added.
Pour and cut

Pour immediately into individual silicone bar moulds (preferred, no cutting required) or a loaf mould. If using a loaf mould, do not insulate, salt bars overheat easily. Cut into bars within six hours, before the salt hardens the loaf fully. Wear gloves when cutting.
Unmould and cure
Unmould after 24 hours. Arrange bars on a rack. Salt bars cure faster than standard bars: four weeks is typically sufficient. The
superfat
at 20% keeps the bar conditioning despite the high salt content.
Using salt bars

Lather the bar in the hands or on a loofah rather than rubbing it directly on the face, the density and salt content make direct use on delicate skin rough. The bar works well for body scrubbing, feet, and rough patches.
Storage and shelf life

Store on a draining soap dish, salt attracts moisture and a bar sitting in water will develop surface beads of brine. Three years or more in a dry cupboard. Discard if rancid patches appear or the bar smells sharp.
